definitions.sense: the first letter of the English alphabet
a note in Western music:
examples: This concerto is in the key of A major.

definitions.sense: a mark in an exam or for a piece of work that shows that your work is considered excellent:
examples: She got straight As (= all her marks were As)
Jim is a straight-A student (= all his marks are A)
Sophie got an A for English.

definitions.sense: used before a noun to refer to a single thing or person that has not been mentioned before, especially when you are not referring to a particular thing or person:
examples: I've bought a car.
She's got a boyfriend.
There was a sudden loud noise.
What a shame that you couldn't go to the party.
I heard a child crying.
Is he a friend of yours (= one of your friends)

definitions.sense: used to say what type of thing or person something or someone is:
examples: She wants to be a doctor when she grows up.
This is a very mild cheese.
Experts think the painting may be a Picasso (= one done by Picasso)

definitions.sense: used to mean any or every thing or person of the type you are referring to:
examples: Can you ride a bike?
A cheetah can run faster than a lion.
A teacher needs to have a lot of patience.

definitions.sense: used before some uncountable nouns when you want to limit their meaning in some way, such as when describing them more completely or referring to one example of them:
examples: I only have a limited knowledge of Spanish.
He has a great love of music.
There was a fierceness in her voice.

definitions.sense: used before some nouns of action when referring to one example of the action:
examples: Take a look at this, Jez.
I'm just going to have a snack.

definitions.sense: used when referring to a unit or container of something, especially something you eat or drink:
examples: I'd love a coffee.
All I had for lunch was a yogurt.

definitions.sense: used before the first but not the second of two nouns that are referred to as one unit:
examples: a cup and saucer
a knife and fork

definitions.sense: used before some words that express a number or amount:
examples: a few days
a bit of wool
a lot of money

definitions.sense: used in front of a person's name when referring to someone who you do not know:
examples: There's a Ms Evans to see you.

definitions.sense: used in front of someone's family name when they are a member of that family:
examples: Is that a Wilson over there?

definitions.sense: used before the name of a day or month to refer to one example of it:
examples: My birthday is on a Friday this year.
It's been a very wet June.

definitions.sense: one:
examples: a hundred
a thousand
a dozen
There were three men and a woman.

definitions.sense: used between a fraction and a unit of measurement:
examples: half a mile
a quarter of a kilo
three quarters of an hour
six tenths of a second

definitions.sense: used when saying how often something happens in a certain period:
examples: Take one tablet three times a day.
I swim once a week.

definitions.sense: used when saying how much someone earns or how much something costs in a certain period:
examples: She earns $100,000 a year.
My plumber charges £30 an hour.
I pay £25 a week for my parking permit.

definitions.sense: written abbreviation for amp
in or for each or every; per:
examples: Take one tablet three times a day.
These shoes cost $30 a pair.

in Western music, the sixth note in the scale (= series of notes) that begins on the note C, or a set of notes based on this note
a mark that means excellent, given to something of the highest quality, esp. school work:
examples: The teacher gave me an A for my essay.

definitions.sense: to leave a place, thing, or person, usually for ever:
examples: We had to abandon the car.
By the time the rebel troops arrived, the village had already been abandoned.
As a baby he was abandoned by his mother.
We were sinking fast, and the captain gave the order to abandon ship.

definitions.sense: to stop doing an activity before you have finished it:
examples: The game was abandoned at half-time because of the poor weather conditions.
They had to abandon their attempt to climb the mountain.
The party has now abandoned its policy of unilateral disarmament.

definitions.sense: to allow yourself to be controlled completely by a feeling or way of living:
examples: He abandoned himself to his emotions.

definitions.sense: in a completely uncontrolled way:
examples: We danced with wild abandon.

definitions.sense: to leave behind or run away from someone or something, or to give up something:
examples: Air attacks forced the villagers to abandon their homes.
The weather was so bad, we abandoned our plans for a picnic.

definitions.sense: to stop an activity before it is finished, usually because you think you cannot succeed:
examples: The car maker has abandoned its plans to build a giant new plant.
The high cost of legal representation can influence a person's decision about whether to abandon a claim.

definitions.sense: to leave a person, place, or thing that needs you to care for them:
examples: He kept the company going because he didn't want to abandon his staff.
A vehicle had been abandoned on the side of the road.

definitions.sense: to allow an insurance company to keep property that has been lost or damaged, in exchange for an insurance payment
the physical or mental power or skill needed to do something:
examples: There's no doubting her ability.

a mixed-ability class

definitions.sense: used to form nouns from adjectives ending in "-able" to mean the quality of being the stated adjective:
examples: suitability
vulnerability

definitions.sense: the mental or physical power or skill needed to do something:
examples: They should not be taking in somebody they don't have the ability to care for.
Her teammates respect her abilities.

definitions.sense: the power or skill needed to do something, or the fact that someone is able to do something:
examples: There's no doubting her ability.
A good leader has the ability to motivate people.
We like our employees to have a broad range of abilities, not just good qualifications.

definitions.sense: to have the necessary physical strength, mental power, skill, time, money, or opportunity to do something:
examples: Will she be able to cope with the work?

definitions.sense: to find it easier to do something:
examples: Get a good night's sleep and you'll feel better able to cope.

definitions.sense: intelligent or good at what you do:
examples: an able child/student/secretary
This problem is now being looked at by some of the ablest minds/scientists in the country.

definitions.sense: added to verbs to form adjectives that mean able to receive the action of the stated verb:
examples: breakable
washable
movable

definitions.sense: added to verbs to form adjectives that mean worth receiving the action of the stated verb:
examples: an admirable person
an acceptable answer

definitions.sense: having what is needed to do something, esp. the physical or mental power, skill, time, money, or opportunity:
examples: I lost my job and wasn’t able to afford my old apartment.
We won’t be able to keep up this kind of effort much longer.

definitions.sense: good at what you do:
examples: He is an able student.

definitions.sense: to end an activity or custom officially:
examples: I think bullfighting should be abolished.
National Service was abolished in the UK in 1962.

definitions.sense: to put an end to something, such as an organization, rule, or custom:
examples: Massachusetts voters abolished rent control.

definitions.sense: to end an activity, custom, etc. completely or by law or official action:
examples: Educationalists have called on the government to abolish tax on computers.
The government has pledged to abolish child poverty by 2020.

definitions.sense: the intentional ending of a pregnancy:
examples: Abortion is illegal in some countries.
She decided to get an abortion.
She had an abortion when she was a teenager.

definitions.sense: the early, unintentional ending of a pregnancy when a baby or young animal is born too early and dies before it is fully developed:
examples: We expect to see late abortions and birth abnormalities as a result of the radiation leak.
The virus can cause spontaneous abortion in cattle.

definitions.sense: something considered to be a complete failure or to be extremely bad or ugly:
examples: This is an abortion of truth.
One local man described the new building as "an abortion".

definitions.sense: on the subject of, or connected with:
examples: He's always going on about what a great job he's got.

a film about the Spanish Civil War

There's something special/strange/unique about him (= in his character)

definitions.sense: to take action to solve a problem:
examples: I wish you'd do something about your bedroom - it's a real mess.

definitions.sense: positioned around a place, often without a clear purpose or order:
examples: Their belongings were flung about the room.

definitions.sense: in a particular place:
examples: Do you have such a thing as a pen about you/your person? (= Do you have a pen?)
She was puttering about the kitchen.

definitions.sense: a little more or less than the stated number or amount:
examples: about six feet tall
about two months ago
"What time are you leaving work today?" "About five."

definitions.sense: almost:
examples: We're about ready to leave.
Well, I think that's about it for now (= we have almost finished what we are doing for the present)

definitions.sense: in many different directions:
examples: They heard someone moving about outside.
I've been running about all morning trying to find you.

definitions.sense: positioned around a place, often without a clear purpose or order:
examples: She always leaves her clothes lying about on the floor.

definitions.sense: in or near a place:
examples: Is John about (= somewhere near)

definitions.sense: to be going to do something very soon:
examples: I was about to leave when Mark arrived.

definitions.sense: on the subject of; connected with:
examples: "What’s that book about?" "It’s about the Civil War."

There’s something about her attitude that worries me.

definitions.sense: a little more or less than a specific number; approximately:
examples: He’s about six feet tall.
It happened about two months ago.
I’ve had just about enough of your complaining (= I do not want to hear any more)

definitions.sense: almost ready to do something, or intending to do something soon:
examples: He looked as if he was about to burst into tears.
I’m not about to apologize to him.

definitions.sense: positioned or moving in or near a place:
examples: Reporters stood about, waiting for more news.

definitions.sense: in or to a higher position than something else:
examples: There's a mirror above the sink.
He waved the letter excitedly above his head.
She's rented a room above a shop.
Her name comes above mine on the list.
The helicopter was hovering above the building.
It's on the shelf just above your head.
A crack had started to appear just above the light on the ceiling.

definitions.sense: more than an amount or level:
examples: Rates of pay are above average (= greater than average)
It says on the box it's for children aged three and above.
Temperatures rarely rise above zero in winter.
She values her job above her family.
They value their freedom above all else.

definitions.sense: most importantly:
examples: Above all, I'd like to thank my family.

definitions.sense: in a more important or advanced position than someone else:
examples: Sally's a grade above me.

definitions.sense: too good or important for something:
examples: No one is above suspicion in this matter.

definitions.sense: When used in a piece of writing, "above" means higher on the page, or on a previous page:
examples: Please send the articles to the address given above.
The letter was sent to the above address.

definitions.sense: all the people or things listed earlier:
examples: All of the above (= everyone listed earlier)
Once we've finished all of the above we can start on the next project.

definitions.sense: higher than, more than, or at a level greater than:
examples: The helicopter was hovering above the building.
Temperatures here rarely rise above freezing in winter.
Our wages are above average.
I could hardly hear him above the blare of the music.

definitions.sense: In writing, above can mean as stated higher up on this page or on a previous page:
examples: Refer to the diagram shown above.

definitions.sense: To be above doing something is to consider yourself too important or too moral to do it:
examples: He’s not above lying to protect himself.

definitions.sense: those mentioned earlier:
examples: All of the above are to be included.

definitions.sense: in or to a foreign country or countries:
examples: We always go abroad in the summer.
He's currently abroad on business.

definitions.sense: outside, or not at home:
examples: Not a soul was abroad that morning.

definitions.sense: used to say that ideas, feelings, and opinions are shared by many people:
examples: There's a rumour abroad that she intends to leave the company.

definitions.sense: in or to a foreign country or countries:
examples: They used to go abroad every summer.

definitions.sense: the fact of not being where you are usually expected to be:
examples: A new manager was appointed during her absence.
I'll be gone for two weeks, with Chris handling the deliveries in my absence.
She has had repeated absences from work this year.

definitions.sense: the fact of not existing:
examples: He drew attention to the absence of concrete evidence against the defendant.
In the absence of (= because there were not)

definitions.sense: the state of not being somewhere, or a period in which you are not somewhere:
examples: She has had repeated absences from school this year.

definitions.sense: An absence can also be a lack of existence:
examples: He drew attention to the absence of any solid evidence against the defendant.

definitions.sense: a time when someone is not at work or at the place they are expected to be:
examples: Her absence from the meeting was noted.
His fellow directors voted in his absence to fire him.
The worst day for workplace absences is Monday.

definitions.sense: the fact that something is not where it is needed or expected:
examples: The business was suffering from an absence of an overall plan for moving forward.
In the absence of any alternative, we'll continue in the same way as before.

definitions.sense: not in the place where you are expected to be, especially at school or work:
examples: John has been absent from school/work for three days now.
We drank a toast to absent friends.

definitions.sense: not existing:
examples: Any sign of remorse was completely absent from her face.

definitions.sense: used to describe a person or the expression on a person's face when they are thinking about other things and are not paying attention to what is happening near them
without:
examples: Absent a detailed plan, the project was doomed from the start.

definitions.sense: to not go to a place where you are expected to be, especially a school or place of work:
examples: You cannot choose to absent yourself (from work/school) on a whim.
With a brief apology, he absented himself from the table.
I took the opportunity to absent myself from the room.
She made a habit of absenting herself from the family.
The school is not responsible - these students chose to absent themselves.

definitions.sense: not at work or at the place where you are expected to be:
examples: Anna's been absent from work for four days with flu.

definitions.sense: not existing in a particular place:
examples: Any mention of prices is conspicuously absent from the ad, which makes me think they are high.

definitions.sense: very great or to the largest degree possible:
examples: a man of absolute integrity/discretion
I have absolute faith in her judgment.
There was no absolute proof of fraud.

definitions.sense: used when expressing a strong opinion:
examples: He's an absolute idiot!
That's absolute rubbish!

definitions.sense: true, right, or the same in all situations and not depending on anything else:
examples: an absolute law/principle/doctrine
Do you think there's such a thing as absolute truth/beauty?
Her contribution was better than most, but in absolute terms (= without comparing it with anything else)

definitions.sense: An absolute ruler has unlimited power:
without limit, very great, or to the largest degree possible:
examples: She demanded absolute silence.
The day was an absolute (= complete)

definitions.sense: certain; not to be doubted:
examples: Health insurance is an absolute necessity.

definitions.sense: very great or to the largest degree possible:
examples: The board said they had absolute confidence in the CEO, despite the company's difficulties.

definitions.sense: used when expressing a strong opinion:
examples: It's an absolute disgrace!

definitions.sense: completely:
examples: I believed/trusted him absolutely.
You must be absolutely silent or the birds won't appear.
We've achieved absolutely nothing today.

definitions.sense: used for adding force to a strong adjective that is not usually used with "very" or to a verb expressing strong emotion:
examples: It's absolutely impossible to work with all this noise.
The food was absolutely disgusting/delicious.
I absolutely loathe/adore jazz.

definitions.sense: used as a strong way of saying "yes":
examples: "It was an excellent film, though." "Absolutely!"

definitions.sense: used as a strong way of saying "no":
examples: "Are you too tired to continue?" "Absolutely not!"

definitions.sense: completely; beyond any doubt:
examples: You are absolutely right.
Are you absolutely sure that you locked the front door?

definitions.sense: Absolutely is also used in conversation to show emphasis in agreeing to something:
examples: "Can you lend me $10 till tomorrow?" "Absolutely, it’s no problem."

definitions.sense: If you say absolutely not, you are showing emphasis in not agreeing to something:
examples: "You mean you won’t sign this?" "No, absolutely not."

definitions.sense: to take something in, especially gradually:
examples: Our countryside is increasingly being absorbed into large cities.
The drug is quickly absorbed into the bloodstream.
Plants absorb carbon dioxide.
In cold climates, houses need to have walls that will absorb heat.
Towels absorb moisture.
Vitamin D gets synthesized when the sun's ray get absorbed by the skin.

definitions.sense: to reduce the effect of a physical force, shock, or change:
examples: The barrier absorbed the main impact of the crash.

definitions.sense: to understand facts or ideas completely and remember them:
examples: It's hard to absorb so much information.

definitions.sense: to take up someone's attention completely:
examples: The project has absorbed her for several years.

definitions.sense: if a business absorbs the cost of something, it pays that cost easily:
examples: The school has absorbed most of the expenses so far, but it may have to offer fewer places next year to reduce costs.

definitions.sense: if one company absorbs another company, it takes control of it and they become one company:
examples: Telecorp Holdings absorbed its Spanish subsidiary into its British headquarters.

definitions.sense: to take in a liquid, gas, or chemical:
examples: The black clay soil around here doesn’t absorb water very well.

definitions.sense: to completely take the attention of someone:
examples: She was absorbed in listening to music.

definitions.sense: To absorb knowledge, ideas, or information is to understand them completely and store them in your memory:
examples: It was difficult to absorb so much information.

definitions.sense: if an organization absorbs the cost of something, it pays that cost:
examples: The law school has absorbed most of the expenses so far, but it may have to offer fewer places next year to reduce costs.

definitions.sense: if one company absorbs another company in a takeover, they become one company:
examples: Telecorp Holdings absorbed its Spanish subsidiary, Digital Corporation, into its British headquarters.

definitions.sense: existing as an idea, feeling, or quality, not as a material object:
examples: Truth and beauty are abstract concepts.

definitions.sense: An abstract argument or discussion is general and not based on particular examples:
examples: This debate is becoming too abstract - let's have some hard facts!

definitions.sense: general ideas:
examples: So far we've only discussed the question in the abstract (= without referring to any real examples)
I have difficulty dealing with the abstract - let's discuss particular cases.

definitions.sense: used to refer to a type of painting, drawing, or sculpture that uses shapes, lines, and colour in a way that does not try to represent the appearance of people or things:
examples: abstract art
an abstract painter

definitions.sense: a short form of a speech, article, book, etc., giving only the most important facts or ideas:
examples: There is a section at the end of the magazine that includes abstracts of recent articles/books.

definitions.sense: a painting that uses shapes, lines, and colour in a way that does not try to represent the appearance of people or things
to consider something in a general way or make a general judgment after looking at particular details:
examples: Most interviewees focus on their own experience and do not generalize or abstract the situation.

definitions.sense: to remove or separate someone or something from a place or context (= the situation, facts, words, etc. that exist around something):
examples: It was impossible to abstract children from their social environment with all its dangers.
Relevant information was abstracted from the database or from medical records.

definitions.sense: to give a summary or abstract (= a short description giving the most important ideas) of something:
examples: If you find an article you think should be abstracted in our journal, submit it for consideration.

definitions.sense: existing as an idea, feeling, or quality, not as a material object:
examples: "Humanity" is an abstract idea.

definitions.sense: If a statement, argument, or discussion is abstract, it is general and not based on particular examples.

examples: abstract art

definitions.sense: a few sentences that give the main ideas in an article or a scientific paper
existing as an idea, feeling, or quality, not as a material object:
examples: "Satisfaction" is difficult to measure as it is an abstract concept.

definitions.sense: a shortened form of a speech, article, book, etc., giving the most important facts or ideas:
examples: There is a section at the end of the magazine which includes abstracts of recent articles.

definitions.sense: stupid and unreasonable, or silly in a humorous way:
examples: What an absurd thing to say!
Don't be so absurd! Of course I want you to come.
It's an absurd situation - neither of them will talk to the other.
Do I look absurd in this hat?

definitions.sense: things that happen that are stupid or unreasonable:
examples: The whole situation borders on the absurd.
She has a keen sense of the absurd.

definitions.sense: ridiculous or completely unreasonable:
examples: It is absurd for the council to cut taxes without proposing another way to raise money.

definitions.sense: the situation in which there is more than enough of something:
examples: There was an abundance of food at the wedding.
This team has talent in abundance.
The area has an abundance of lakes, rivers, and streams to fish in.

definitions.sense: the quality of having what you want in life, for example, love, happiness, or career success:
examples: I am trying to manifest abundance in all areas of my life.
Incorporating affirmations into your morning routine sets the tone for a day filled with prosperity and abundance.

definitions.sense: an amount that is more than enough:
examples: We all seem to have an abundance of those plastic grocery bags.
Grapes and olives grow in abundance in the valley.

definitions.sense: the level of a particular element in the outer layer of the earth
to use something for the wrong purpose in a way that is harmful or morally wrong:
examples: She is continually abusing her position/authority by getting other people to do things for her.
I never expected that he would abuse the trust I placed in him.
He fears that his brother may be abusing alcohol.

definitions.sense: to treat someone cruelly or violently:
examples: The therapist works with children who have been sexually abused.
The dog showed signs of being physically abused.
Men who abuse their partners are good at portraying themselves as the real victims.

definitions.sense: to speak to someone rudely or cruelly:
examples: The athlete was being verbally abused by a drunk fan in the crowd.
The crowd started abusing him after he failed to save a goal.

definitions.sense: the use of something in a way that is harmful or morally wrong:
examples: The investigation revealed abuses of power committed by the governor's office.

definitions.sense: cruel, violent, or unfair treatment of someone:
examples: She claimed to have been a victim of child abuse.

definitions.sense: bad or cruel treatment of a person or animal, or the use of something in an unsuitable or wrong way:
examples: The rescued dogs had been victims of physical abuse.

definitions.sense: to treat a person or animal badly or cruelly, or to use something in the wrong way:
examples: He was always welcome but he never abused the privilege by visiting us too often.

definitions.sense: a situation in which a person uses something in a bad or wrong way, especially for their own advantage or pleasure:
examples: The former president has been accused of corruption and abuse of power.

definitions.sense: rude and offensive words said to another person:
examples: He claimed he had received verbal abuse from his co-workers.

definitions.sense: to use something in a bad or wrong way, especially for your own advantage or pleasure:
examples: The Chief Executive is accused of abusing his position by advising family members when to buy and sell shares.
Workers found to be abusing drugs or alcohol will be offered help.

definitions.sense: to use rude and offensive words to another person:
examples: Striking workers abused colleagues who continued to go into work.

definitions.sense: relating to schools, colleges, and universities, or connected with studying and thinking, not with practical skills:

definitions.sense: used to describe someone who is clever and enjoys studying:
examples: I was never a particularly academic child.

examples: The debate about whether this is a recession has become purely academic.

definitions.sense: someone who teaches at a college, or who studies as part of their job
the subjects that you study in high school or college:
examples: Her son seems to prefer sports over academics.

definitions.sense: relating to schools, esp. colleges and universities, or connected with studying and thinking and not with useful skills
not important because it is based only on possibilities:
examples: Which diamond ring you like more is purely academic, because I can’t afford either one.

definitions.sense: a person who teaches in a college or university

examples: Employers nowadays are more interested in candidates' abilities and personality rather than just academic qualifications.

definitions.sense: interested in studying and successful at school work:
examples: Like many entrepreneurs, he was not particularly academic at school.

definitions.sense: a person who teaches at a college, or who studies as part of their job:
examples: The research company was founded by a group of academics from Stockholm University.

definitions.sense: an organization intended to protect and develop an art, science, language, etc., or a school that teaches a particular subject or trains people for a particular job:
examples: the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art

definitions.sense: the part of a sports club or team that trains young players who might one day become professional:
examples: The youth academy starts training talented young players from the age of eight.

definitions.sense: a school in the UK that is not controlled by the local authority and receives its money directly from the central government

examples: a military/police academy

definitions.sense: When a vehicle or its driver accelerates, the speed of the vehicle increases:
examples: I accelerated to overtake the bus.

to happen or make something happen sooner or faster:
examples: Inflation is likely to accelerate this year, adding further upward pressure on interest rates.

definitions.sense: to move more quickly, or to make something happen faster or sooner:
examples: He stepped on the gas and accelerated rapidly to pass a car.

definitions.sense: to make something, esp. a process or a very small piece of matter, move faster
to go faster or make something go faster:
examples: The car can accelerate to 60 miles per hour in just 6 seconds.
Inflation is likely to accelerate this year, adding further upward pressure on interest rates.

definitions.sense: the way in which people in a particular area, country, or social group pronounce words:

examples: She teaches an extension class on computer technology.

definitions.sense: a new part that is added onto a building:

definitions.sense: in a way that covers a large area or has a great range:

definitions.sense: area or length; amount:

definitions.sense: the area, length, or size of something:

definitions.sense: added to what is normal:

definitions.sense: more:

definitions.sense: something that you can get with something else if you pay a little more money:

in cricket, a point that a team scores that is not from a hit made by a batter (= a player who tries to hit the ball)
outside or in addition to:

extracurricular activities (= activities which are not part of the usual school or college course)

definitions.sense: added, additional, or more than expected:

extra cash/funding/money
extra compensation/income/pay
extra charge/expense/fee

definitions.sense: to make more effort than is expected of you:

definitions.sense: a substance that has been got from another substance, using a particular process:

definitions.sense: very unusual, special, unexpected, or strange:

definitions.sense: very large in amount or degree:

definitions.sense: at the furthest point, especially from the centre:

definitions.sense: at the furthest point; to the greatest degree:

definitions.sense: Extreme opinions, ideas, etc., are beyond the usual range of variety and would seem unreasonable to most people.
the first or fourth terms (= numbers or symbols) of a proportion (= a mathematical statement with a comparison of two numbers calculated by division on each side):

definitions.sense: very:

definitions.sense: very:

the hole in a needle through which you put the thread

definitions.sense: the structure or parts of something:

definitions.sense: cloth or woven material, or a type of this material:

definitions.sense: imaginary, not existing in real life:

to deal with a difficult situation:

Many short rivers flow into the Pacific Ocean.
The river flows through three counties before flowing into the sea just south of here.
With fewer cars on the roads, traffic is flowing (= moving forward)

definitions.sense: to continue to arrive or be produced:
examples: Please keep the money flowing in!
Offers of help are flowing into the disaster area from all over the country.
My thoughts flow more easily if I work on a computer.
By eleven o'clock, the wine was starting to flow.
After they'd all had a drink or two, the conversation began to flow.

definitions.sense: to hang down loosely and often attractively:
examples: Her long red hair flowed down over her shoulders.

definitions.sense: the movement of something in one direction:
examples: the flow of a river
the flow of traffic
the flow of blood

definitions.sense: a regular and quite large number of something:
examples: There's been a steady flow of visitors.

definitions.sense: a situation in which something is produced or moved continuously:
examples: the flow of ideas/information

definitions.sense: a pleasant state in which someone is giving their attention completely to what they are doing, not thinking about anything else, and doing it skilfully and easily:
examples: Flow is sometimes referred to as "being in the zone".

definitions.sense: a man's long hair, especially that of an athlete :
examples: His blond locks give him some incredible flow, making him one of the most recognizable players in the league.

definitions.sense: (esp. of liquids, gases, or electricity) to move in one direction, esp. continuously and easily:
examples: Air flows over an aircraft’s wing faster than it flows under it.

definitions.sense: Something can be said to flow if it hangs down loosely and attractively:

definitions.sense: supported by or resting at the top of another thing:

definitions.sense: attached to or forming a part of another thing:

definitions.sense: covering or wrapping another thing:

definitions.sense: being broadcast:

I wish there were more jazz on the radio.

definitions.sense: used to show a method of travel; via:

Two people rode by on horseback.

definitions.sense: at, near, or next to a particular place, thing, or person:

definitions.sense: used to show the form in which information is stored or recorded for use with an electronic device:

definitions.sense: showing what tool, instrument, system, etc., is used to do or achieve something:

definitions.sense: showing that a drug is taken or used:

definitions.sense: used after some verbs and adjectives to show that help is needed from a person or thing:

definitions.sense: used to show that a condition or process exists or is being experienced:

definitions.sense: involved in or doing a particular thing:

definitions.sense: connected with or part of a group or process:

definitions.sense: about or having something as a subject:

definitions.sense: showing that something is paid for or how something is paid for:

definitions.sense: used to show when something happens:

definitions.sense: possessing, carrying, or having something with you now:

definitions.sense: continuing or not stopping:

definitions.sense: toward or to something or someone:

definitions.sense: happening or planned:
